openingProblem.problem: In 1956 both Poland and Hungary turned to reform Communists who had been imprisoned under Stalin. Poland got a new leader; Hungary got Soviet tanks. What decided the difference?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: why was Hungary invaded and Poland not?
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which piece of evidence most changed or confirmed it?

chunks.title: 1953: the first protests after Stalin
chunks.body:
Most people in Soviet eastern Europe, Tony Judt writes, accepted their fate without protest in the early 1950s. The exceptions came in the most industrial corners of the bloc, and only after Stalin's death in March 1953.

In Czechoslovakia a "currency reform" of 31 May 1953 cut industrial wages by 12 per cent once prices rose. Twenty thousand workers at the Škoda plant in **Plzeň** demonstrated, and on 1 June thousands marched on the city hall carrying portraits of the pre-Communist presidents Beneš and Masaryk. The protest was contained in one city and fizzled out.

A few days later a far larger protest broke out in **East Germany**. The regime imposed large unpaid increases in the work "norms", the output each worker had to produce, and ignored Moscow's advice to compromise in order to stop skilled workers fleeing to the West. On 16 June 1953 some 400,000 workers went on strike across the country, with the largest demonstrations in Berlin. The East German police could not cope alone. Red Army tanks were called in; nearly 300 people were killed, 1,400 received long prison sentences and 200 "ringleaders" were shot. Bertolt Brecht asked in a poem whether it would be simpler for the government "to dissolve the people and elect another one".

These were workers' protests about pay and conditions, not national revolutions, and Judt argues they "hardly represented a threat to Soviet power". But Moscow took them seriously. Stalin's heirs now faced a problem: how to end the worst of Stalin's terror without endangering the system it had built. In Hungary, at Moscow's own initiative, the Stalinist leadership of Mátyás Rákosi was replaced in July 1953 by the reformer Imre Nagy. Nagy closed the internment camps and let peasants leave the collective farms. Under Rákosi some 480 public figures had been executed and over 150,000 people imprisoned in a country of fewer than 9 million.

This mattered because the first response to unrest was reform from above, which meant that the satellites learned that Moscow's line could change. When Rákosi persuaded Moscow in 1955 that Nagy could not be trusted, Nagy was removed. The pattern of the next three years was set: reform when Moscow allowed it, retreat when Moscow withdrew it.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The 1953 protests were economic, set off by wage cuts and higher work norms.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Marchers in Plzeň carried portraits of Beneš and Masaryk, so there was a political edge.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Force ended them, but the Red Army had to be called in.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Nearly 300 deaths show the protest was serious, though Judt argues it never threatened Soviet power.

argumentsThatWork.claim: After Stalin's death Moscow tried reform from above, as with Nagy in Hungary.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Nagy's removal in 1955 showed how limited and reversible that reform was.

howItGetsAsked: Evaluate the causes and consequences of the East German uprising of 1953.

useItInAnEssay.claim: The East German uprising of June 1953 was caused above all by economic grievances that the regime itself had made worse.
useItInAnEssay.prove: The government imposed large unpaid increases in work norms and ignored Moscow's advice to compromise, and on 16 June some 400,000 workers struck.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that a regime more rigid than its Soviet masters turned a dispute over pay into a challenge to its authority.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the rising was suppressed only when Red Army tanks were called in, with nearly 300 killed, which shows how little the regime could rely on its own forces.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The uprising was therefore economic in cause but political in consequence: it proved the GDR depended on Soviet force.

chunks.title: 1956: the secret speech and the Polish October
chunks.body:
Nikita Khrushchev's strategy after 1953 had four parts, Judt explains: calm relations with the West, rebuild bridges to Yugoslavia (he visited Belgrade in May 1955), encourage reformers in the satellites and end the show trials, and finally break with Stalin himself. The last step came at the Twentieth Party Congress. On 25 February 1956, in his **"secret speech"**, Khrushchev denounced Stalin's crimes and personality cult. His aim was to protect the system by blaming one man.

The speech could not be kept secret. It leaked within weeks. Together with the dissolution of the Cominform on 18 April and the reconciliation with Tito, it seemed to tell eastern Europe that Moscow would now accept different "roads to socialism" and had given up terror. This mattered because it encouraged people to believe that change was permitted, which meant that every satellite regime now faced pressure from below that Moscow had itself unleashed.

**Poland** felt it first. In June 1956 the Polish army put down demonstrations in **Poznań** sparked, like East Berlin's, by disputes over wages and work-rates. Discontent spread through the autumn. In October the Polish party removed the Soviet Marshal Konstanty Rokossovsky as defence minister and chose as First Secretary **Władysław Gomułka**, a Communist who had been imprisoned under Stalin. To Poles he was the national face of Communism; to Moscow his election looked like defiance.

On 19 October Khrushchev, Mikoyan, Molotov and other leaders flew to Warsaw uninvited, while Soviet tanks moved towards the capital. In tense talks, some of them on the airport tarmac, Gomułka assured them that he would keep control, would not leave the Warsaw Pact and would not ask Soviet troops to leave. Khrushchev decided he could live with him. He told his colleagues that the Soviet ambassador had been "grossly mistaken" about Gomułka, who was a sound party man.

Judt concludes that the "Polish October" had a "fortuitously benign outcome": few knew how close Poland had come to a second Soviet occupation. Gomułka understood the limits. De-Stalinisation did not mean that Moscow would give up its influence or the party its monopoly. Personnel could change and public life could relax; the party's leading role and the alliance could not.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The secret speech, meant to protect the system, encouraged demands for change across the bloc.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: It was meant for the party elite, and in Czechoslovakia it produced no political action.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Gomułka saved Poland from invasion by keeping the party in control and Poland in the Warsaw Pact.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Khrushchev also feared that force in Poland would provoke violent confrontation.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Economic grievances lit the fuse in Poland as in East Germany.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The election of Gomułka was a national, political act, not an economic one.

howItGetsAsked: Discuss the view that de-Stalinisation caused the crises of 1956 in Poland and Hungary.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Gomułka avoided a Soviet invasion because he offered Moscow what it cared about most: party control and the alliance.
useItInAnEssay.prove: On 19 October 1956, with Soviet tanks moving towards Warsaw, he assured Khrushchev that he would keep control, stay in the Warsaw Pact and not ask Soviet troops to leave.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that Moscow could accept new leaders and some liberalisation, because the two foundations of its control were untouched.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, Khrushchev also feared that forcing matters would almost certainly provoke violent confrontation in Poland.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Gomułka's guarantees were therefore the decisive reason the Polish October ended peacefully.

chunks.title: Hungary 1956: revolution and invasion
chunks.body:
In Hungary the story ended differently. Moscow removed Rákosi on 17 July 1956 but replaced him with another Stalinist, Ernő Gerő, who could neither lead change nor suppress it. On 6 October the regime allowed the public reburial of László Rajk and other show-trial victims; Judt calls it the spark of the revolution. On 16 October students in Szeged formed an independent league; on 22 October Budapest students issued Sixteen Points, demanding free speech, reforms, Nagy as prime minister and the withdrawal of Soviet troops.

On **23 October** students gathered in Budapest. That evening, after Gerő denounced them on the radio, crowds tore down the statue of Stalin and Soviet troops entered the city. The next morning Imre Nagy was named Prime Minister. He declared martial law, but he could not stop a revolution that was creating its own workers' councils and national committees across the country. On 28 October he proposed a truce, recognised the protests as revolutionary, promised to abolish the secret police and announced that Soviet troops would leave Budapest. On 30 October he announced a government based on the parties of 1945: the end of one-party rule.

Moscow hesitated. On 31 October the Soviet leadership even declared itself ready to negotiate troop withdrawals. But reports of student protests in Romania and unrest among Bulgarian intellectuals raised fears that revolt would spread. On 1 November Khrushchev told his colleagues that withdrawal would look like weakness. Soviet divisions moved towards Hungary; Nagy protested by declaring Hungary **neutral** and withdrawing from the Warsaw Pact. That same evening János Kádár was taken to Moscow to head a new government. At 4 a.m. on **4 November** Soviet tanks attacked Budapest.

Resistance was intense, but the city fell within three days. About 2,700 Hungarians died in the fighting. Afterwards 341 were executed, some 22,000 imprisoned and 13,000 interned; about 200,000 people, over 2 per cent of the population, fled abroad. Nagy took refuge in the Yugoslav embassy, was abducted when he left, and was executed after a secret trial on 16 June 1958.

The West did nothing. A July 1956 US policy paper had already said the United States was "not prepared to resort to war" to end Soviet domination, although Radio Free Europe encouraged the rebels to fight. Britain and France were absorbed in the Suez crisis, and Eisenhower in his re-election. This mattered because the Hungarians learned that no one would help them, which meant that after 1956, in Judt's words, the dominant mood in the bloc was "cynical resignation".

argumentsThatWork.claim: The invasion came when Nagy abandoned the party's monopoly and left the Warsaw Pact.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Moscow had been willing to negotiate on 31 October; fear of contagion changed its mind.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The revolution was popular and national, driven by students and workers' councils, not by Nagy.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Nagy's announcements gave it legitimacy; he was 'swept up' as much as he led.
The West had decided long before 1956 that it would not fight for the satellites.

howItGetsAsked: To what extent was Nagy's abandonment of the party's monopoly of power responsible for the Soviet invasion of Hungary in 1956?
Compare and contrast the crises in Poland and Hungary in 1956.

useItInAnEssay.claim: The Soviet invasion of Hungary was caused above all by the collapse of the party's monopoly of power.
useItInAnEssay.prove: On 30 October 1956 Nagy announced a government based on the coalition parties of 1945, and on 1 November he declared Hungary neutral and outside the Warsaw Pact.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the two foundations of Soviet control, one-party rule and the alliance, were both abandoned, so Moscow faced a precedent that could spread.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, as late as 31 October the Soviet leaders were ready to negotiate withdrawal, and what changed their minds was fear of unrest in Romania and Bulgaria.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The end of one-party rule made intervention likely, but the fear of contagion made it certain.

chunks.title: Why Poland and Hungary ended differently, and the Berlin Wall
chunks.body:
Poland and Hungary both began 1956 with reform-minded Communists returning from disgrace. Why was one country invaded and the other not? Judt's answer is precise. Moscow could accept new leaders, liberalisation and even talk of national roads to socialism. What the Kremlin could not condone was the abandonment of the party's **monopoly of power**, "something Gomułka, in Poland, had taken care never to allow". Nagy's multi-party government was "the thin edge of a democratic wedge" that threatened every Communist party. That is why the other satellite leaders supported the invasion so readily, and why even Tito, briefed on 2 November, was anxious but understanding.

The aftermath created a new kind of stability. In Hungary Kádár, after harsh reprisals, offered a bargain: Hungarians were allowed a limited but real freedom to produce and consume, and in return were asked only to abstain from opposition. This "goulash Communism" secured Hungary's stability, and the memory of 1956 stabilised the rest of the bloc for a decade. The price, Judt argues, was that socialism lost its promise and became "just a way of life to be endured".

East Germany had a different problem: people could leave. Between 1949 and August 1961 between 2.8 and 3 million East Germans, about 16 per cent of the population, crossed to the West through Berlin, many of them young and educated. From November 1958 Khrushchev used Berlin as a lever, demanding an end to the Western occupation regime there; his real aim, Judt argues, was to stop West Germany gaining nuclear weapons. The crisis dragged on to 1961 and the exodus became a flood: 30,415 people left in July 1961 and 21,828 more in the first week of August.

In August 1961 Moscow authorised the East Germans to close the border across Berlin. Within days a rough wall stood; it was then strengthened with barbed wire, searchlights and guard posts. The West protested in public, but many Western leaders were privately relieved: a wall was better than a war. At Vienna in June Kennedy had already signalled that the United States did not wish to deprive the USSR of its ties in eastern Europe.

This mattered because the Wall stopped the flight that threatened the GDR's survival, which meant that Soviet control now rested on physically enclosing a population that Judt calls the subjects of a "weak and unloved" regime.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Moscow drew the line at the party's monopoly of power, not at reform as such.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Nagy's departure from the Warsaw Pact also mattered, since it threatened the alliance.

argumentsThatWork.claim: After 1956 control rested on a bargain of material goods for political silence.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The bargain followed severe repression, so it rested on fear as well as consent.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Berlin Wall solved the GDR's exodus by force, with the West's quiet acceptance.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Khrushchev's main aim in the Berlin crisis was West German nuclear weapons, not the exodus.

howItGetsAsked: Examine the reasons why the Berlin Wall was built in 1961.
Analyse the methods used by the Soviet Union to maintain control of eastern Europe between 1953 and 1961.

useItInAnEssay.claim: The Berlin Wall was built mainly to stop an exodus that threatened the survival of East Germany.
useItInAnEssay.prove: Between 1949 and August 1961 between 2.8 and 3 million East Germans, about 16 per cent of the population, left through Berlin, and 30,415 went in July 1961 alone.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the GDR was losing its educated young people faster than it could replace them, so without closing the border the state would soon have emptied.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, Judt argues that Khrushchev's Berlin crisis was driven by his wish to stop West Germany gaining nuclear weapons, not by the refugees.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The exodus was therefore the immediate reason for the Wall, while the wider crisis created the moment for it.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: To what extent was Nagy's abandonment of the party's monopoly of power responsible for the Soviet invasion of Hungary in 1956?
essayQuestions.namedFactor: Nagy's abandonment of the party's monopoly of power

decodeKey.verb: To what extent: judge how far
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The end of the party's monopoly, weighed first
decodeKey.judgement: How far this, compared with neutrality, contagion and Western weakness, caused the invasion

modelPlan.thesis: The end of the party's monopoly was largely responsible, because it was the one change Moscow could not accept; but fear of contagion decided the timing, and Western weakness removed the risk.

arguments.claim: The multi-party government ended the leading role of the party (named factor first).
Neutrality and leaving the Warsaw Pact threatened the alliance.
Fear of contagion to Romania and Bulgaria changed Moscow's mind.
Western non-intervention removed the risk.

modelPlan.counter: Neutrality was announced only after Soviet troops were already moving, so the decision to invade came before Hungary left the Pact.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Would Moscow have invaded if the party had kept its monopoly? Poland suggests not, so the monopoly was the decisive factor.

segments.text: The end of the party's monopoly of power was the main reason for the Soviet invasion of Hungary.
On 30 October 1956 Nagy announced a government based on the coalition parties of 1945, and Judt argues that this, not economic reform or censorship, was what the Kremlin could not condone.
This meant that Hungary was becoming a precedent for every satellite, which is why other Communist leaders backed the invasion so readily.
However, as late as 31 October Moscow was ready to negotiate, and it was reports of unrest in Romania and Bulgaria that turned it to force.
The end of one-party rule was therefore the decisive cause, and fear of contagion the trigger.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: “De-Stalinisation caused the crises of 1956 in Poland and Hungary.” Discuss with reference to 1956.

decodeKey.verb: Discuss: test the claim for and against, then judge
decodeKey.scope: The crises in Poland and Hungary
decodeKey.judgement: How far de-Stalinisation, rather than local grievances or leaders, caused the crises

modelPlan.thesis: The claim is largely right that de-Stalinisation made the crises possible, but local grievances triggered them and local choices decided how they ended.

arguments.claim: For: the secret speech and the end of the Cominform suggested national roads were allowed (named factor first).
For: Moscow's own changes of leader in Hungary encouraged reform.
Against: wages and work-rates triggered Poznań.
Against: Rajk's reburial and student demands drove Hungary.

modelPlan.counter: In Czechoslovakia the secret speech produced no political action, so de-Stalinisation alone did not cause crises.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Was de-Stalinisation a necessary condition? Yes, but not a sufficient one, since Czechoslovakia stayed quiet.

segments.text: De-Stalinisation made the crises of 1956 possible by suggesting that Moscow would now accept change.
Khrushchev's secret speech of 25 February leaked within weeks, and with the Cominform dissolved in April it seemed to promise different roads to socialism.
This meant that people and party reformers believed protest might succeed, so grievances that had been suppressed came into the open.
However, in Czechoslovakia the memory of terror was too fresh for the speech to produce any action, so de-Stalinisation alone was not enough.
De-Stalinisation was therefore a necessary cause of the crises, but local grievances and choices decided their course.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Evaluate the causes and consequences of the East German uprising of 1953.

decodeKey.judgement: Which cause mattered most, and which consequence was most significant

modelPlan.thesis: The uprising was caused mainly by economic grievances made worse by a rigid regime; its main consequence was to show that the GDR depended on Soviet force, which fed the exodus that later produced the Wall.

arguments.claim: Cause: unpaid increases in work norms.
Cause: the regime ignored Moscow's advice after Stalin's death.
Consequence: repression by Red Army tanks.
Consequence: workers fled West, adding to the exodus.

modelPlan.counter: Judt argues the rising never threatened Soviet power, so its consequences were limited.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which consequence lasted longest? The proof that the regime needed Soviet tanks, which shaped the GDR until 1989.

segments.text: The East German uprising was caused above all by economic grievances that the regime had made worse.
The government imposed large unpaid increases in work norms, ignored Moscow's advice to compromise, and on 16 June some 400,000 workers struck.
This meant that a regime more rigid than its masters turned a dispute over pay into a challenge to its authority.
However, Judt argues the rising hardly threatened Soviet power, since it was crushed within days.
Its main significance was therefore to expose the GDR's dependence on Soviet force.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast the crises in Poland and Hungary in 1956.

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences, explicitly linked
decodeKey.judgement: Which difference explains the different outcomes

modelPlan.thesis: Both crises grew from de-Stalinisation and brought back reform Communists, but they ended differently because Gomułka kept the party's monopoly and the alliance while Nagy gave up both.

arguments.claim: Similarity: de-Stalinisation and local grievances.
Similarity: the return of Communists purged under Stalin.
Difference: Gomułka kept control and the alliance.
Difference: Nagy accepted pluralism and neutrality, and Hungary was invaded.

modelPlan.counter: Khrushchev also feared a violent confrontation in Poland, which is larger, so the outcome reflected Soviet calculation as well as local choices.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which difference decided the outcome? The party's monopoly, which Judt calls the Kremlin's red line.

segments.text: The crises in Poland and Hungary began alike but ended in opposite ways.
In Poland Gomułka assured Khrushchev on 19 October that he would keep control and stay in the Warsaw Pact, whereas Nagy announced a multi-party government on 30 October and neutrality on 1 November.
This meant that Poland kept the two things Moscow cared about, while Hungary abandoned both, so only Hungary appeared to threaten the bloc.
However, both crises grew from de-Stalinisation, and in both the parties turned to men purged under Stalin.
The decisive difference was therefore the party's monopoly of power, not the strength of popular protest.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Examine the reasons why the Berlin Wall was built in 1961.

decodeKey.verb: Examine: break the issue into parts and consider their interrelationship
decodeKey.scope: The building of the Berlin Wall

modelPlan.thesis: The Wall was built mainly to stop an exodus that threatened the GDR's survival; the Berlin crisis provided the moment, and Western acceptance removed the risk.

arguments.claim: The exodus: 2.8–3 million left by 1961.
Khrushchev's Berlin crisis from 1958.
Western signals of acceptance.
Shoring up a weak and unloved regime.

modelPlan.counter: Khrushchev's real aim in the crisis was West German nuclear weapons, so the Wall was a by-product of a different conflict.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Without the exodus, would the Wall have been built? Almost certainly not, so it was the decisive reason.

segments.text: The Berlin Wall was built mainly to stop an exodus that threatened the survival of the GDR.
Between 1949 and August 1961 between 2.8 and 3 million East Germans left through Berlin, and 30,415 went in July 1961 alone.
This meant the state was losing its young and educated faster than it could replace them, so closing the border was a matter of survival.
However, Judt argues that Khrushchev's Berlin crisis was driven by his wish to stop West Germany gaining nuclear weapons.
The exodus was therefore the decisive reason, while the crisis created the opportunity.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Analyse the methods used by the Soviet Union to maintain control of eastern Europe between 1953 and 1961.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into parts and show how they connect
decodeKey.judgement: Which method was decisive and how they combined

modelPlan.thesis: Moscow combined force, reform from above and enclosure: tanks in 1953 and 1956, managed change through trusted Communists, and the Berlin Wall; force was decisive, but reform and material concessions made control durable.

arguments.claim: Force: East Germany 1953 and Hungary 1956.
Reform from above through trusted Communists: Nagy (1953), Gomułka (1956).
Material concessions for political silence: goulash Communism.
Enclosure: the Berlin Wall.

modelPlan.counter: Reform from above was itself a source of instability, as Hungary showed.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which method, if removed, would have ended control? Force, since every other method rested on the threat of it.

segments.text: Soviet control between 1953 and 1961 rested ultimately on force, but Moscow also used managed reform to reduce the need for it.
Red Army tanks crushed the East German rising in 1953 and took Budapest in 1956, while Moscow accepted Gomułka in Poland once he promised to keep control.
This meant that reform was allowed where the party kept its monopoly and force was used where it did not, so the threat of tanks set the limits of change.
However, after 1956 Kádár's goulash Communism showed that material concessions could secure stability without constant force.
Force was therefore the foundation of control, with reform and concessions making it last.
